item.title: There Is an "I" in Team
item.description:
Sport and Competition

There Is an "I" in Team

The challenge of pursuing excellence without turning competition into a battle.

Posted June 7, 2026

Key points
  • Sport and competition hold a tension between the pressure to prove our value and our need to belong as we are.
  • Healthy teams invite each individual's values, goals, and skill set into the collective vision.
  • Instead of a battle, competition can become a shared challenge and a way to pursue excellence together.
Novak Djokovic and Alexander Zverev.
Source: Francesco Panunzio/Shutterstock

Sports, and especially team sports, embody many values we hold dear—hard work, commitment, the pursuit of competence, teamwork, camaraderie, and working together toward a shared goal. They give us the chance to navigate challenge, rely on others for support, offer support in return, and experience being part of something where we feel valued, seen, and included, and a sense of belonging.

For me, this is one of the most powerful possibilities of sport and competition. They give us a place to develop these values while also learning how we respond to the pressure to perform, be evaluated, and belong.

Interestingly, the root of the word competition comes from the Latin competere, meaning to seek, strive, or come together in pursuit of something. In this original sense, more than defeating an opponent, competition carries the idea of coming together around a shared challenge.

When I reflect on my childhood, sport and being part of a team originally felt like that. Competition was about play, friendship, shared effort, learning, challenge, and belonging. It was about practicing something over and over again, until we became competent in it, and confident we could repeat it, even under pressure. It was about the joy of being part of something, working together, and discovering what we could become was more than I could pull off on my own.

But somewhere along the way, that experience began to change. It started to become about being better than someone else, earning my spot, or proving my value. It became less about fun, exploration, and curiosity, and more about winning, performing well, and not falling short.

This is part of the inherent tension in team sports. We are working together toward a shared goal, while also competing with our own teammates for roles, recognition, playing time, leadership, or the chance to be the one with the ball when the moment matters most. That tension is real at every level of sport.

Managing the Tension Between Competition and Belonging

The question is how we recognize and respect this tension without allowing it to organize the player, the team, and the team culture around fear, comparison, and conditional belonging.

Can we create environments where competition still motivates us, but does not separate us from ourselves or one another? Can we pursue excellence without making belonging dependent on performance? Can we respect the reality of selection, roles, and standards while still feeding the biological benefits of shared effort, support, trust, and unconditional belonging?

This is one of the most important possibilities of sport. Sport gives us a living experiment in how to hold both truths at once: the pressure to perform and the need to belong; the drive to compete and the need to connect; the pursuit of winning and the biological quest for safety, trust, and support just as we are.

Sport gives us the chance to work hard at something, get better at something, and belong to something. But there is also the pressure to earn our role, win a spot, or prove our value. In many ways, we can feel only as good as our last performance.

When we learn to hold this tension more consciously and honestly, team sport becomes more than a place to win, acquire, or conquer. Although we may have to fight at times, it is not a quest to dominate or destroy. Instead, it becomes a place to practice being human. It becomes an environment for sharing pressure together, sometimes leading, sometimes following, and sometimes battling alongside one another, but always being part of something.

The Importance of the Individual "I" in Team Dynamics

We often hear that there is no “I” in team. But there must be. An effective team is not built by erasing the individual, but by including each “I” in the collective. We give voice, dignity, and value to each teammate. We respect the biological needs and responses of each body. We create the conditions where individual differences contribute to the shared vision, purpose, and potential of the group.

When the “I” is encouraged and welcomed into the “we,” the team can become more than a battlefield where roles, status, and belonging are constantly being fought for. It can grow into a place where effort, purpose, and belonging can be experienced together. Where each member of the team is met exactly where they are. And where we commit to competence and competition not as a way to acquire something for ourselves, but as a way to contribute to something bigger than ourselves.

This capacity is part culture, part perspective, and part physiology. We need a capacity to feel safe enough, resourced enough, and already enough to compete not as an attempt to acquire something we lack, but as an expression of something we already have. Culture, perspective, and physiology all play a role, either supporting or interrupting this process.

This same capacity can be cultivated not only in team sports, but also in individual sports like tennis or golf. The opponent does not have to become the enemy standing in our way. Instead, they can be seen as someone just like us, committed to the craft, sharing similar values and goals, and feeling the same pressures to perform. In that sense, the opponent can become an opportunity, much like a teammate, to elevate our potential and pursue a level of competence we couldn’t reach on our own. We recognize the sameness within our differences.

When we meet competition this way, the opponent is no longer simply someone to defeat, and the teammate is no longer simply someone to outperform. Sport becomes an experiment, a place to practice what it means to be human. Competition becomes a chance to pursue excellence and challenge ourselves without compromising connection, belonging, and the deeper reasons that brought us to the game in the first place.

Would we still love watching and playing sports if players and teams were not fighting for their lives or trying to dominate and destroy one another? Would we still be moved by the courage of putting it all out there, the commitment to showing up, the contrasting styles of play, the creativity and problem-solving, and the unexplainable momentum shifts and comebacks? Would we still be drawn to the beautiful, imperfect, and unpredictable qualities that make the game, and the athlete, so compelling?

I know I would.

item.title: The Importance of Love in Life
item.description:
Personal Perspectives

The Importance of Love in Life

Personal Perspective: Lucy Dillon, a brave heroine, loved her husband despite trials.

Posted June 7, 2026

Key points
  • Rereading "Bluebird, or the Invention of Happiness," I was struck by Lucy Dillon's courage and intelligence.
  • Yet what impressed me above all was her love for her husband despite the dire difficulties of their lives.
  • I realized I had endowed my heroine with a love of my own.

I am rereading one of my own books, which has recently been republished by Open Road: Bluebird, or the Invention of Happiness. It is based on the life of the Marquise de la Tour du Pin, an Irishwoman who married a French marquis and escaped the French Revolution of 1789, thanks to her great courage. It was she who obtained the permits to leave France from Tallien, the fierce revolutionary. The family sailed from France in a one-masted boat, going to Boston during the winter months with their two small children. Lucy Dillon, which was her maiden name, was a source of inspiration to me. Brave, intelligent, and always curious, this woman of Irish origin came to America and kept her family alive by becoming a dairy farmer in the Albany area.

Yet rereading my own book about her, what struck me most was that this was above all a love story. Whoever Lucy was in real life, I had made her in love with her French husband, Frederick. Lucy, in my version of her, loved her husband despite the great difficulties of their life together. The Marquis de la Tour du Pin does not take to farming in America as Lucy does. He does not appreciate the freedom of their life on the farm, and prefers his career in France as a soldier and his books. The moment he can, he insists on their return to France to reclaim his ancestral chateau. Frederick is not a practical man and it is mainly thanks to Lucy's intervention with Napoleon that the Marquis becomes a Prefect in Amiens. Lucy accompanies him to the Fort du Ha when he refuses to sign the papers of allegiance to Phillipe d'Orleans. Lucy and Frederick have six children, all of whom die except for one boy. Lucy eventually loses all her properties—Frederick is not good with money, her money, and she finds herself living alone in Pisa after Frederick's death at the end of her life with her only boy.

Yet through all of this adversity, her ultimate allegiance is to Frederick. She loves him from the first moment she sees him as an adolescent when he comes to ask for her hand from her grandmother at her house on the Rue du Bac. Lucy gives birth to her little girl, Seraphine, whom Frederick catches during the birth and then has to leave precipitously, to avoid capture. Separated from him during the days of the revolution in France, she longs for her Frederick and greets him with great joy when he is able to join her for their voyage to America.

Rereading my own words, I realized how much of my own love for my husband of 40 years lies in this book. What a gift he has given me remaining at my side all this time. And how important our love for all family—our children, our partners—is.

item.title: Emotion and Meaning in the Social World
item.description:
Emotions

Emotion and Meaning in the Social World

Emotions mediate social interactions, for better and for worse.

Posted June 7, 2026

Key points
  • Our responses to one another are essentially emotional.
  • Long before the development of sophisticated language, humans used emotions to communicate.
  • Emotions may be more contagious than any known virus.
  • We continually make implicit value judgments in the social world.

Our responses to one another are essentially emotional. Our emotions automatically react to the emotional states of others, inferred from their appearance, scent, expressed ideas, beliefs, and behavior. The following are mechanics of emotional interaction.

How Emotions Were Used for Preverbal Communication

Long before the development of sophisticated language, humans used emotions to communicate and to serve as a social alarm system. We sensed in one another important messages like:

“The saber tooth tigers are coming!”
“The elk are leaving!”
“Let's go in this direction.”
“Let's mate!”

Each emotion retains primitive non-verbal display characteristics to inform the world. These include facial expressions (smiles, frowns, glares), vocalizations (cooing, moaning, sobbing, screaming, roaring), changes in posture and muscle tone (slumping, tensing, imminent springing, or fleeing), and various expressive behaviors such as stomping feet, beating one’s breast, and pulling one’s hair.

With the development of sophisticated language, the need for emotional display waned, along with our tolerance of it. The uninhibited display of emotions is rare in people over three years old.

Cultural Norms Governing Emotional Displays

Most cultures tolerate raw emotional displays by adults only under clearly defined circumstances of ceremony or extremity. The display of anguish, for example, includes weeping, wailing, and flailing, with a sharply down-turned mouth forming the ancient mask of tragedy. That's okay at a funeral, not in a theater. A shame display includes slumped head (neck muscles weaken making eye contact difficult), hands covering a flushed face, and constricted muscles, as the shamed person contorts to the smallest space possible. (The root of the word “shame” means to cover or hide.) The display of anger includes bulging, dilated eyes, tightened jaw, exposed teeth, tense muscles, menacing body posture, and either deepened or shrieking voice. These are natural displays which must be inhibited or suppressed in most social situations.

Attempts to suppress emotional display do not work as well with involuntary muscles, especially of the face, or with tone of voice. We do not hide anger, resentment, or fear as well as we think we do, as they manifest , albeit subtly, in facial expressions, body language, and tone of voice.

Contagion: No One is an Island

Emotions are more contagious than any known virus. Happy people tend to make us happy, caring people make us care, interested people attract our interest, and sports events lacking excited spectators bore us. We try to avoid those who carry “chips on their shoulders,” who “bring us down,” or “overwhelm us.”

Resentment and subtle hostility spread workstation by workstation throughout the office or factory and locker by locker in schools. Aggressive driving passes car by car down the highway.

Contagion also accounts for “group think,” which makes people act collectively against their individual better judgments. It gives us constantly changing fashions, cultural fads, and political correctness. It produces solidarity parades, protest marches and, on the uglier side, “mob justice,” public lynching, riots, and looting.

Related to the law of contagion is the principle of reciprocity. Allowing for differences of inhibition and temperament, we get back more or less the same emotional intensity we put out.

How Emotions Lead to Projection

While experiencing intense emotions, it’s virtually impossible to read other people's emotions with any accuracy. When our own internal experience is strong, we merely project it onto others. For example, the resentful person is likely to project resentment or untrustworthiness on others. The extreme example is the paranoid person who projects negative emotions on everyone.

Negative projections almost inevitably become self-fulfilling prophecy. We’re likely to resent someone who thinks we’re resentful and suspect someone who feels we’re untrustworthy.

Social Value Judgments Mitigate Emotional Contagion

To attenuate the effects of contagion, we regularly employ social value judgments, mostly based on presumed intellectual, emotional, or spiritual superiority. Social value judgments carry an illusion of predicting and controlling the behavior of others, which provides a sense of safety. (Unpredictable behavior raises anxiety, even when harmless. Think of your response when someone disrobes in public or shouts on the subway.) The predictability of perceived dangers and our control over them determine perceptions of safety. For instance, soldiers can feel safe during hostilities if confident of their combat skills, which allow them to predict and control threats to safety. The same soldiers can feel unsafe in peacetime when combat skills have little utility.

The primary instrument of social control is shame-inducing moral reprobation. We describe failures to sustain pro-social emotions like compassion and remorse as “inhumane” and hold deficits of sincerity and trustworthiness in contempt and disgust.

We use the law of social value judgment to guide our own behavior to a much lesser extent than we apply it to others. We tend to judge other people’s behavior in moral terms and our own in terms of utility—it works for us. Similarly, while we’re hypersensitive to unfair treatment by others, we’re hardly sensitive at all to our own unfairness, which takes determined self-reflection. In other words, our judgment of others is easy and automatic, while self-reflection takes focus, energy, and determination.

item.title: The AuDHD Strength of Being Heartfelt
item.description:
Neurodiversity

The AuDHD Strength of Being Heartfelt

Experiencing the world through sincerity and belonging.

Posted June 7, 2026

Key points
  • Heartfelt AuDHD expression reflects authenticity and commitment to personal values.
  • Thoughtful decision-making strengthens purpose, identity, and well-being.
  • Heartfelt awareness includes sensitivity to fairness, trust, and integrity.

This post is the fourth in a five-part series exploring strengths associated with coexisting autism and ADHD. Without minimising the real challenges of AuDHD, the series draws on clinical practice and research to highlight strengths from a person-centred, strengths-based perspective. If you’d like to read the previous articles in this series, you can find them here: Part 1, Part 2, and Part 3.

In my article Understanding Strengths With Coexisting Autism and ADHD (Storace, 2025), which considers the strengths associated with coexisting autism and ADHD, I described five interconnected capacities: attuned, unified, dynamic, heartfelt, and driven. Among these, the quality of being heartfelt speaks most directly to how individuals relate to themselves, to others, and to the values that guide their lives (Taylor et al., 2023).

Heartfelt expression reflects something deeper than emotional sensitivity alone. It involves authenticity, sincerity, ethical awareness, and a strong desire to live in alignment with what feels true. This article highlights how Heartfelt Strength is experienced in everyday life.

Understanding “Heartfelt” as a Strength

To be heartfelt is to engage with the world through authenticity and sincerity. While many social environments encourage people to adapt, perform, or present versions of themselves that fit expectations, heartfelt individuals feel most comfortable when they can communicate openly and relate genuinely.

For many people with AuDHD, this quality emerges alongside a strong awareness of fairness, sincerity, and emotional truth. They can be highly sensitive to inconsistency between what people say and what they do. Relationships tend to feel meaningful when they are based on frankness, trust, and mutual respect rather than social convention alone (Milton, 2012).

Four Dimensions of the Heartfelt Experience

Heartfelt: Genuine Human Connection
Source: Keith Storace

1. Authentic Self-Expression

Authenticity involves communicating in ways that reflect what one genuinely thinks, feels, and believes. Honesty, transparency, and consistency become important features of interpersonal engagement. Connection generally feels most comfortable when it is grounded in truthfulness rather than performance (Milton, 2012). Although direct communication can occasionally be misunderstood when it does not conform to expected social conventions, it can also foster respect and relationships characterised by sincerity and mutual understanding.

2. Sensitivity to Fairness

Awareness of fairness shapes how situations, relationships, and social systems are interpreted. Exclusion, inequality, hypocrisy, and inconsistency may be identified quickly, particularly when actions appear misaligned with stated values or expectations. When in conversation with people with AuDHD, I’ve noticed that this awareness is often accompanied by a strong commitment to inclusion, equitable treatment, and individual dignity. While concern for fairness may sometimes be interpreted as idealism, it actually reflects a desire for consistency between values and behaviour, as well as a willingness to question practices that appear unjust or exclusionary.

3. Values-Guided Decision-Making

Decision-making is usually informed by an internal set of values that provides direction and purpose. Questions such as "Does this feel right?" or "Is this consistent with who I am?" can carry significant weight when navigating choices, relationships, and life transitions. Decisions are evaluated through the lens of personal alignment, with external approval carrying less influence. Values-based decision making provides stability and resilience, particularly during periods of uncertainty. When actions remain aligned with personal values, a stronger sense of purpose, identity, and wellbeing follows (Taylor et al., 2023).

4. Trust-Based Relationships

Trust is a key element in building the foundations of interpersonal relationships. Enduring friendships, supportive partnerships, and strong professional relationships can grow from this foundation. The emphasis is not solely on emotional warmth, but on creating conditions in which openness, respect, and psychological safety can develop naturally over time.

Heartfelt Strength in Education

In educational settings, Heartfelt Strength reveals itself through a deep connection to people, values, and purpose. Students with this quality are motivated not only by achievement but also by a desire for their learning to feel meaningful and relevant. They often:

  • Learn best in environments where they feel respected and understood
  • Respond strongly to fairness and consistency
  • Become deeply engaged when learning connects with human issues and real-world scenarios
  • Struggle in classrooms characterised by humiliation, excessive criticism, or relational disconnection

Practical Implications for Education

Learning is often enriched when relationships and values are recognised alongside academic achievement. To support students with heartfelt qualities, educators can:

  • Create emotionally safe and respectful learning environments
  • Model fairness and consistency
  • Encourage discussions about ethics, values, and social responsibility
  • Encourage authenticity and integrity through respectful and inclusive classroom practices

Heartfelt Strength in Employment

In workplaces, employees with heartfelt qualities bring integrity, trustworthiness, and values-based leadership. While these qualities are not always immediately visible, they frequently influence organisational culture in significant ways. Their contribution extends beyond task completion, helping create workplaces where people feel valued, respected, and safe. Employees who express Heartfelt Strength often:

  • Prioritise ethical standards and fairness
  • Build trusting professional relationships
  • Advocate for inclusive and respectful workplaces
  • Thrive in roles involving care, education, counselling, leadership, advocacy, community development, and human services

Practical Implications for Employers and Organisations

People with AuDHD who express heartfelt qualities help strengthen organisational integrity. They are seen as respected leaders and champions of the values that underpin a workplace. These strengths can be fostered by:

  • Encouraging psychologically safe workplaces
  • Recognising ethical leadership at all levels
  • Valuing authenticity as well as achievement
  • Supporting staff who advocate for fairness and inclusion

AuDHD Way of Being

The AuDHD strength of being heartfelt reminds us that strengths can be found not only in what people achieve or produce but also in the standards they set for themselves, the principles they uphold, and the relationships they seek to build. Heartfelt expression contributes something enduring: A commitment to living in ways consistent with deeply held convictions. It reflects a determination to remain fully oneself while participating in the shared human experience.

This post is the fourth in a five-part series exploring strengths associated with coexisting autism and ADHD. Without minimising the real challenges of AuDHD, the series draws on clinical practice and research to highlight strengths from a person-centred, strengths-based perspective. If you’d like to read the previous articles in this series, you can find them here: Part 1, Part 2, and Part 3.
